name: Chalcolepidius webbi
intro: My adults had dark metallic green backs bordered with white, bright enough to pick them out at a glance in a clear rearing cup. This southwestern click beetle gave me one of my clearest observations of where a female lays. I found eggs on bark and on paper towel, and I raised adults from eggs in about a year.

facts.title: Range
facts.text: California, Arizona and New Mexico, south to Sonora and Durango

facts.title: Egg to adult in my culture

sections.title: Eggs
sections.text: In my culture, C. webbi females laid on pieces of bark or on paper towel. These were the first surfaces I checked for eggs. The Alaus I was rearing alongside them laid into the substrate. Looking for the eggs in the right place mattered because the young larvae were so small that they became difficult to recover once dispersed.

sections.title: Larvae
sections.text: The first two instars of the click beetles I raised were about the size of springtails, and cannibalism was common. I separated the larvae early, despite the work involved in finding and moving them. When recording a brood I distinguish the number of larvae I recover from the number of eggs a female may have laid.

sections.title: Adults
sections.text: I photographed a developing beetle in its rearing cup in May 2023. By June I could show four adults together, with the white bands standing out clearly against the green. The interval from egg to maturity in my culture was about a year. Published specimens show variation in the width of the pale markings. Some have white scales over much of the pronotum or wing covers.
